passages.t: Circumcise your hearts, and the lion leaves his thicket
passages.happening:
God sets out the terms of return. If Israel will return, put away idols and stop wavering, and swear by the living LORD ‘in truth, in justice, and in righteousness’ (verse 2), then the nations will find their good in him and glory in him (verse 2).

‘Break up your unplowed ground, and do not sow among the thorns’ (verse 3). ‘Circumcise yourselves to the LORD, and remove the foreskins of your hearts’ (verse 4). Otherwise God's wrath will burn like fire with no one to put it out.

Then the alarm. They are to blow the ram's horn across the land and run to the walled towns (verse 5), and raise a signal flag toward Zion. ‘For I am bringing disaster from the north, and terrible destruction’ (verse 6). ‘A lion has gone up from his thicket, and a destroyer of nations has set out’ (verse 7). They are to put on sackcloth and mourn (verse 8). The king and officials will lose heart, and the priests and prophets will be stunned (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Circumcision was the covenant sign given to Abraham, a mark in the body meant to show belonging to God. To circumcise the heart meant to cut away whatever made the heart closed to God. Deuteronomy had already used the picture. Unplowed ground was hard, crusted earth; seed thrown on it, among thorns, came to nothing.

The ram's horn, the shofar, was blown to warn of attack, and people in the open country fled to walled towns. A signal flag raised on a hill told them which way to run.

The foe from the north is never named in these chapters. Some older scholars suggested Scythian raiders from the steppes. Most today think Jeremiah meant Babylon from the start, or that these poems came to be understood of Babylon when its army came. Babylon lay east, but its armies reached Judah by the northern road through Syria.
passages.later: Moses had said, ‘Circumcise your hearts, therefore, and stiffen your necks no more’ (Deuteronomy 10:16), and Paul writes that true ‘circumcision is a matter of the heart’ (Romans 2:29).
passages.asks: God asks his people to break up the hard ground of their hearts. Ask where your heart has grown crusted and closed. And ask what it would mean to swear by the LORD in truth, justice and righteousness, all three at once.

passages.t: A searing wind, and the prophet's anguish
passages.happening:
Jeremiah cries out that God has deceived the people by promising peace while a sword is at their throats (verse 10).

A searing wind from the desert heights blows toward the people, ‘but not to winnow or to sift’ (verse 11). It is too strong for that, and it comes from God (verse 12). The enemy advances like clouds, with chariots like the whirlwind and horses swifter than eagles (verse 13). ‘Wash the evil from your heart, O Jerusalem, so that you may be saved’ (verse 14). A voice sounds from Dan, then from the hills of Ephraim (verse 15). An army surrounds Judah's cities ‘like men guarding a field’ (verse 17). Their own ways have brought this, and it pierces to the heart (verse 18).

“My anguish, my anguish! I writhe in pain! Oh, the pain in my chest!” (verse 19). Jeremiah cannot be silent, for he hears the horn of battle. Disaster follows disaster, and his tents are destroyed in a moment (verse 20). God says his people are fools who do not know him, ‘skilled in doing evil, but they know not how to do good’ (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
The searing wind is the hot east wind that blows off the desert in spring and autumn and withers plants. When farmers winnowed grain they tossed it into a gentle breeze so the chaff blew away. This wind is too strong for winnowing. It flattens everything.

Verse 15 traces the enemy's advance. Dan, at the source of the Jordan, was Israel's northernmost town, and the hill country of Ephraim lies just north of Jerusalem. The news comes from Dan, then from Ephraim, as the invader moves south toward the capital.

In verse 19 the voice is Jeremiah's own, and it is a cry of physical pain. The prophet does not announce judgment from a safe distance. He feels it in his body.
passages.later: Isaiah also uses the picture of chaff blown away (Isaiah 41:16). Paul grieves for his own people in the same way: ‘I have deep sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart’ (Romans 9:2).
passages.hard:
In verse 10 Jeremiah says God has deceived the people by promising peace. Does God deceive?

Interpreters take it in two main ways. Many read it as Jeremiah's anguished protest, not a doctrine. In his shock he blames God for the false prophets' message of peace, which the book elsewhere says God never sent (14:13-15; 23:16-17). Others note that in Hebrew thought God is often spoken of as the final cause of what he permits, so that when people prefer lies, God can be said to give them over to the deception they chose (1 Kings 22:19-23; 2 Thessalonians 2:11).

On either reading the book does not teach that God lies. It records a prophet's honest cry, and it lays the false promise of peace at the feet of the prophets who spoke it.
passages.asks: Jeremiah could not be silent about what he saw coming. Ask whether there is a danger you see that you have kept quiet about. And ask whether you are skilled at doing good, or only at noticing what is wrong.

passages.t: Creation undone, and Zion gasping for breath
passages.happening:
‘I looked at the earth, and it was formless and void; I looked to the heavens, and they had no light’ (verse 23). The mountains quaked and the hills swayed (verse 24). ‘I looked, and no man was left; all the birds of the air had fled’ (verse 25). The fruitful land was a desert, and its cities torn down before the LORD's anger (verse 26).

‘The whole land will be desolate, but I will not finish its destruction’ (verse 27). The earth will mourn and the heavens grow dark (verse 28).

Every city flees at the sound of horsemen and archers (verse 29). And Zion, devastated, dresses in scarlet and gold and paints her eyes, but her lovers despise her and want her life (verse 30). Jeremiah hears a cry like a woman in labor with her first child, the cry of Zion gasping for breath, stretching out her hands before her killers (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
Verse 23 uses the words of Genesis 1:2, formless and void, the state of the earth before God spoke light. Jeremiah's vision runs creation backward: no light, no people, no birds, no fruitful land. Judah's sin is so deep that it seems to undo the world.

Yet verse 27 keeps a door open. God will not make a full end. Even in the darkest vision there is a remnant.

Zion dressing up for her lovers pictures Judah courting foreign allies who would turn on her. The cry of a woman in labor was the strongest picture of sudden, helpless pain the first hearers knew. These are pictures of a city, not of any woman.
passages.later: The words of verse 23 are those of the first chapter of the Bible: ‘Now the earth was formless and void’ (Genesis 1:2). Isaiah uses the picture of labor pains for those who see judgment coming (Isaiah 13:8).
passages.asks: Even in the vision of a ruined world, God says he will not make a full end. Ask where you need to hear that in your own life. And ask whom you have courted for safety who could not give it.
